title: Tongues, then and now
hook: Pentecostals and charismatics pray in tongues; some Christians believe such gifts ceased, others are open

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fruit of the Spirit: one fruit, many flavors, grown rather than forced. Your line was fruit, not effort.

What does it sound like? In a Pentecostal service the music softens, and around the room people begin to pray aloud, but not in words the visitor next to them can follow. Syllables rise and fall, like a language overheard through a wall. For the people praying, this is a gift of the Spirit. Across town, a pastor teaches that gifts like this belonged to the apostles' time and have ceased. In a third church, people say kindly that they're open, but cautious. Same Bible, three answers.

It starts at Pentecost, in Acts; day one thousand forty-one saw churches wear red for it. A sound like a rushing wind, and "they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Here the crowd understands: visitors from many lands each hear their own language. Corinth seems different. Paul writes that "he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God." Nobody understands without an interpreter. So Paul sets rules: two or three, one at a time, and with no interpreter, keep silent in the church and speak to God privately. And a balance: "covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues." Three answers come out of these pages. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians pray in tongues today, often as a private prayer language, sometimes aloud in worship with interpretation; some Pentecostal churches teach it as the sign of being baptized in the Spirit. Cessationists, in some Reformed and Baptist churches, read the gifts as signs that confirmed the apostles' message and ceased with that age; they point to Paul: "whether there be tongues, they shall cease." Pentecostals answer that the passage puts the ceasing when "that which is perfect is come," which they read as Christ's return. Others sit between: open to the gift, wary of pressure, glad of Paul's rules for order. Each side takes the same chapters seriously. Some Christians reach for John's line: "The wind bloweth where it listeth." In that reading, the Spirit isn't on a leash, in anybody's church.
screen: `PENTECOST: EACH HEARS HIS OWN LANGUAGE.` · `CORINTH: SPEAKING UNTO GOD.` · `FORBID NOT, BUT KEEP ORDER.` · `TODAY, IN USE, CEASED, OR OPEN.` · then, large: `THE WIND BLOWETH WHERE IT LISTETH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a way of praying or worshiping that isn't yours, louder than you'd choose, or quieter, or stranger, and notice what rises: curiosity, discomfort, longing. Don't argue with it; hold open the possibility that something real is happening in rooms you'd never walk into. If you pray, ask for humility toward those who pray differently; if you don't, simply breathe, and let the wind be the wind.
Tongues. Speech given by the Spirit: languages heard at Pentecost, prayer unto God in Corinth, and a question the churches still answer differently.
Your line: the spirit blows. Same Bible, three answers, all taken seriously. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: you're Paul. the church in Corinth is loud with tongues, and visitors can't understand a word. what do you write?

fork.reveal: Paul says let two or three speak in turn, with an interpreter; if there's none, keep silent in church and speak to God. and: "forbid not to speak with tongues."

chat.says: Was speaking in tongues at Pentecost the same as what Paul describes in Corinth?
options: Acts says the crowd heard their own languages; in Corinth no one understood without an interpreter.
Yes. In both places, everyone present understood every word without any help.
No. At Pentecost no one understood, but at Corinth everyone heard their own language.
chat.meaning: At Pentecost visitors heard their own languages. In Corinth, Paul says the speaker speaks unto God, and no one understands without an interpreter.

notes: Acts 2:6 says 'every man heard them speak in his own language'; the voice paraphrases as 'visitors from many lands each hear them in their own language'.

Paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 14:27–28 ('by two, or at the most by three, and that by course; and let one interpret ... let him keep silence in the church; and let him speak to himself, and to God'). Confirm.

Positions described: Pentecostal teaching of tongues as the (initial) evidence of Spirit baptism is held by some Pentecostal bodies, not all; cessationism attributed to 'some Reformed and Baptist churches'; the Pentecostal reading of 13:10 as the end of the age. Confirm fairness and that no side is ranked.
The hook's description of a Pentecostal service is a general picture; confirm it is recognizable and respectful.
Original note: γλῶσσα meaning both tongue and language is a standard lexicon gloss; confirm.
